title: Health Checks & Failover
summary: How a load balancer detects a bad node and routes around it, and the interval, threshold, and draining choices that decide whether that happens fast or safely.

slides.markdown:
A load balancer can only route around a dead server if it knows the server is dead — that's what **health checks** are for. Get the checking wrong and you either keep sending traffic to a broken node for too long, or you yank healthy nodes out of rotation on false alarms.

This topic covers active vs passive checks, tuning intervals and thresholds, draining a node safely instead of dropping requests, and what actually happens during failover.

slides.sectionTitle: Active health checks vs passive health checks
slides.markdown:
An **active health check** is the load balancer proactively pinging each server on a schedule — hitting `/health` every 5 seconds and expecting a 200 OK — independent of whether any real traffic is flowing. It catches a dead server even during a lull with zero user requests.

A **passive health check** watches real traffic instead: if the last N requests to a server timed out or returned 5xx, the load balancer marks it unhealthy without sending any extra probe traffic. It reacts using signal that's already there, but only detects a problem once real users have already hit it.

Production setups typically run both — active checks for fast, traffic-independent detection, passive checks as a backstop that catches failures active checks might miss between polls.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: health check loop pulling a bad node out of rotation
slides.markdown:
![Health checks removing a failed node from rotation](assets/health-check-loop.svg)

The loop is continuous and independent of user traffic: the load balancer polls every node on a fixed interval, and a node that fails enough consecutive checks in a row gets marked unhealthy and removed from the rotation the next routing decision makes.

The node isn't removed after one failed check — that would react to a single dropped packet — it's removed after crossing a configured failure threshold, which is the next slide's trade-off.

assets.alt: Health checks removing a failed node from rotation

slides.sectionTitle: Choosing check intervals and thresholds: flapping vs slow detection
slides.markdown:
Two numbers control every health-check setup: the **interval** (how often to check) and the **threshold** (how many consecutive failures before marking a node unhealthy — and how many consecutive successes before marking it healthy again).

| Setting | Aggressive (short interval, low threshold) | Conservative (longer interval, higher threshold) |
|---|---|---|
| Detects real failure | Fast (seconds) | Slower (tens of seconds) |
| False positives | More likely — one blip pulls a healthy node | Less likely — needs a sustained pattern |
| Risk | **Flapping** — a node bounces in and out of rotation | Traffic keeps hitting a genuinely dead node longer |

**How to decide:** start conservative (e.g. 3 consecutive failures, 10s interval) and tighten only if real incidents show detection was too slow — tuning for the fastest possible detection first tends to cause flapping on ordinary network jitter.

slides.sectionTitle: Connection draining: removing a node without dropping in-flight requests
slides.markdown:
Pulling a node out of rotation the instant it's marked unhealthy (or scheduled for a deploy) can kill requests it's already in the middle of answering. **Connection draining** (also called graceful shutdown) instead stops sending it *new* requests immediately, while letting its in-flight requests finish normally within a timeout window.

Concretely: a node about to be redeployed gets marked "draining," the load balancer stops routing new traffic to it, and after 30 seconds (or when its last connection closes, whichever is first) it's safely removed and can be shut down.

Without draining, every deploy or scale-down event randomly cuts off whatever requests happened to be in flight on that node.

slides.sectionTitle: Failover mechanics: how traffic re-routes when a node dies
slides.markdown:
Once a node is marked unhealthy, failover is mechanically simple: the load balancer just stops including it in whatever algorithm picks the next server — round robin skips it, least connections never considers it, a consistent-hashing ring routes its slice of keys to its ring neighbor instead.

The in-flight requests already on that node are the messy part: if it died outright (not just failed a health check), those requests fail outright and it's up to the client or an upstream retry policy to resend them to a different node. This is why idempotent request design matters upstream of load balancing — a retried request should be safe to run twice.

Recovery mirrors removal: once the node passes enough consecutive health checks again, it re-enters the rotation gradually rather than all at once, to avoid a cold node getting slammed the instant it returns.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: a health check that passes while the app is actually unhealthy
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Our `/health` endpoint returns 200, so the load balancer will correctly keep sending it traffic — the check is working."

**Why it's wrong:** a shallow health check (does the process respond at all?) can pass even when the thing that actually matters is broken — the app can't reach its database, a critical dependency is timing out, or a memory leak has it thrashing under real load while still answering a trivial `/health` ping fast.

**Correct model:** a good health check exercises the dependencies the app actually needs to serve real requests — check that the database connection pool has a live connection, not just that the HTTP server is listening. Shallow checks catch "process crashed"; they miss "process alive but useless," which is the more common real-world failure.

slides.sectionTitle: Real numbers: what production defaults actually look like
slides.markdown:
Concrete defaults anchor the interval/threshold trade-off. AWS's Application Load Balancer defaults to a **30-second** check interval with **3 consecutive failures** to mark unhealthy (90 seconds worst case to detect) and **5 consecutive successes** to mark healthy again — deliberately slower to re-add than to remove, since a flaky recovery is cheaper to wait out than a flaky removal is to flap on. Kubernetes liveness/readiness probes commonly run every **10 seconds** with a **3-failure threshold**, giving roughly 30 seconds worst-case detection inside a cluster, where network jitter between pods is lower than across the public internet.

The pattern across both: **healthy-to-unhealthy is faster than unhealthy-to-healthy** by design — removing a bad node quickly limits blast radius, while re-adding one slowly protects against a node that's still warming up or intermittently flaky right after recovering.

Use these as starting points, not gospel: a stateful service with expensive connection setup (a database) often wants slower removal than a stateless web tier, since yanking it out and back in repeatedly is more disruptive.

slides.sectionTitle: The staff-level nuance: recovery can cause the next outage
slides.markdown:
A subtle failure mode: when several nodes fail together (a deploy gone wrong, a shared dependency recovering) and then all pass their health checks at nearly the same moment, the load balancer can dump full production traffic onto all of them simultaneously — cold caches, cold connection pools, JIT-warmup penalties — and the sudden load re-fails the very nodes that just recovered, sometimes worse than the original outage.

The fix production load balancers use is **gradual re-admission** (sometimes called slow start): a newly-healthy node gets a small fraction of its fair share of traffic initially, ramping up over tens of seconds as it proves it can handle load, rather than jumping straight to 100%. Envoy's `slow_start` config and similar features in most modern proxies exist for exactly this reason.

The senior-level tell: an engineer who says "health checks bring nodes back automatically" is describing the mechanism; one who adds "...and we ramp them back in gradually, because a cold node getting full traffic can re-fail immediately" is describing the mechanism *and* its known failure mode.
